unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which of the following is defined as a collection of elements where each element is accessed in a sequential order?
explanation: In linear data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues), elements form a sequence and each member has a unique predecessor and successor.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which data structure is inherently non-linear?
explanation: Trees and graphs are non-linear data structures because elements are arranged hierarchically or interconnected arbitrarily.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is an Abstract Data Type (ADT)?

options.text: A mathematical model of data objects together with operations defined on them

explanation: An ADT specifies what operations can be performed on data and what values it can hold, without dictating how they are implemented.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which operation involves processing every element in a data structure exactly once?
explanation: Traversing (visiting) visits each element of a data structure systematically to read or process its value.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which asymptotic notation describes the tightest upper bound of an algorithm's running time?
explanation: Big-O notation denotes the upper bound or worst-case running time of an algorithm.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Big-Omega (Ω) notation is primarily used to represent:
explanation: Big-Omega notation defines a lower bound that guarantees an algorithm will take at least that amount of time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Big-Theta (θ) notation represents:

options.text: Asymptotically tight bound (both upper and lower bound)

explanation: Big-Theta binds an algorithm from above and below, representing an exact asymptotic behavior.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the space complexity of an algorithm that allocates a 1D array of size N?
explanation: Storing N elements in memory requires memory proportional to N, giving O(N) space complexity.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which term describes the compromise where an algorithm consumes more memory to run faster?
explanation: The time-space trade-off occurs when an algorithm uses extra storage (like hash tables or lookup tables) to reduce processing time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In C, which property is TRUE regarding standard arrays?

options.text: Arrays allocate contiguous blocks of memory
Array elements can hold different data types
Array bounds are automatically checked at runtime

explanation: Arrays in C store homogeneous elements sequentially in contiguous physical memory addresses.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: If a 1D array A[0..N-1] has base address B and element size w, the address of A[i] is calculated as:
explanation: For a zero-indexed 1D array, Address(A[i]) = Base_Address + (i * element_size).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In row-major order for a 2D array A[1..M, 1..N] with base address B and element size w, the address of A[i, j] is:
explanation: In row-major order, all elements of previous rows ((i-1)*N) are skipped before reaching column (j-1).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In column-major order for a 2D array A[1..M, 1..N] with base address B and element size w, the address of A[i, j] is:
explanation: In column-major order, elements are stored column by column. Address = B + w * ((j - 1) * M + (i - 1)).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which programming language stores 2D arrays in row-major order?
explanation: C, C++, and Python store multi-dimensional arrays in row-major order, whereas FORTRAN and MATLAB use column-major.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: A 2D array A[10][20] in C has base address 2000. Each element takes 2 bytes. What is the address of A[3][5] in row-major order?

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is a Sparse Matrix?

options.text: A matrix where all elements are prime numbers
A matrix where a majority of elements are zero
A matrix whose determinant is strictly negative
A matrix with odd number of rows

explanation: A sparse matrix is a matrix populated primarily with zeros, where storing all elements wastes memory.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In 3-tuple representation of a sparse matrix, what do the three columns represent?

options.text: Row index, Column index, Non-zero Value
Block number, Row count, Column count
Node address, Next pointer, Data value

explanation: A 3-tuple (triplet) stores (Row, Column, Value) exclusively for each non-zero element.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In an N x N Lower Triangular Matrix, which elements are guaranteed to be zero?

options.text: Elements on the main diagonal (i == j)

explanation: In a lower triangular matrix, all elements strictly above the main diagonal (where row index i < column index j) are zero.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: How many non-zero elements can an N x N lower triangular matrix have at most?
explanation: Row 1 has 1 element, row 2 has 2, ..., row N has N elements. Total = sum(1..N) = N*(N+1)/2.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is a Tri-diagonal Matrix?

options.text: A matrix where non-zero elements exist only on the main diagonal and the adjacent diagonals immediately above and below it
A matrix with exactly three rows
A matrix with zero diagonal elements

explanation: In an N x N tri-diagonal matrix, elements A[i][j] can be non-zero only if |i - j| <= 1.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the maximum number of non-zero elements in an N x N tri-diagonal matrix?
explanation: Main diagonal has N elements, upper sub-diagonal has N-1, and lower sub-diagonal has N-1 elements. Total = N + (N-1) + (N-1) = 3N - 2.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: When adding two sparse matrices represented as 3-tuples, the time complexity is proportional to:

options.text: Product of their total entries (M * N)
Sum of their non-zero elements (k1 + k2)

explanation: Addition scans both sorted triplet lists once using a merge-like process taking O(k1 + k2) time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In a 3D array A[P][M][N] stored in row-major order, which dimension varies fastest in memory?
explanation: In row-major order, the rightmost index (last dimension N) varies fastest in contiguous memory.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which data structure is the most efficient for frequent insertions and deletions at arbitrary positions?
explanation: Linked lists avoid shifting elements because insertion/deletion merely involves pointer updates, taking O(1) once position is located.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of accessing an element in an array by its index?
explanation: Array indexing computes the exact memory address via base address arithmetic in constant O(1) time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What happens if a program attempts to write beyond the allocated bounds of an array in C?

options.text: The compiler generates a syntax error
Undefined behavior (possible memory corruption or segmentation fault)

explanation: C does not perform runtime array bound checking, resulting in undefined behavior or memory violations.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: If an algorithm's time complexity is T(N) = 3N^3 + 5N^2 + 100, its Big-O notation is:
explanation: In asymptotic analysis, constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped, leaving O(N^3).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which algorithm complexity class grows the fastest as N increases?
explanation: Factorial time O(N!) grows faster than exponential O(2^N), polynomial O(N^2), and linearithmic O(N log N).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which notation represents the function f(N) such that there exist positive constants c and n0 with 0 <= c*g(N) <= f(N) for all N >= n0?
explanation: This is the formal mathematical definition of Big-Omega (Ω) notation for asymptotic lower bounds.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: For an upper triangular matrix of size N x N, elements A[i][j] are zero when:
explanation: In an upper triangular matrix, all elements strictly below the main diagonal (where row index i > column index j) are zero.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In a sparse matrix representation, the header triplet (row 0) typically stores:

options.text: Total rows, Total columns, Total non-zero count
Base address, Pointer size, Data type
Null terminator, First index, Last index

explanation: The first record of a triplet sparse matrix denotes the matrix dimensions (rows, cols) and total non-zero entries.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the memory saved by storing an N x N symmetric matrix as a 1D array compared to a full 2D array?
explanation: Since A[i][j] == A[j][i], only N*(N+1)/2 elements need to be stored instead of N^2, saving roughly half the space.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In an algorithm with two sequential independent loops, one running N times and another M times, the overall time complexity is:
explanation: For independent sequential loops, their execution times add up: O(N) + O(M) = O(N + M).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the time complexity of transposing an N x N matrix stored as a conventional 2D array?
explanation: Transposing visits all N*N matrix cells, leading to O(N^2) time complexity.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: The fast transpose algorithm for a sparse matrix in 3-tuple format achieves a time complexity of:
explanation: Fast transpose counts elements per column and computes starting positions, transposing in O(Columns + Non_Zero) time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which of the following functions exhibits logarithmic growth?
explanation: Binary search repeatedly divides the search range by half, yielding O(log N) time complexity.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: An algorithm that takes time proportional to 2^N is classified as having:
explanation: O(2^N) represents exponential time, common in brute-force recursive solutions to combinatorial problems.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which data structure provides constant O(1) time insertion and deletion at both ends?
explanation: A Deque supports push_front, push_back, pop_front, and pop_back in O(1) constant time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: The recurrence relation T(N) = T(N/2) + O(1) corresponds to which time complexity?
explanation: By the Master Theorem (Case 2 with a=1, b=2, d=0), T(N) = O(log N), typical of binary search.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the primary drawback of using contiguous arrays for dynamic data collections?

options.text: Accessing elements by index is slow
Fixed size requiring expensive reallocation and copying when capacity is exceeded
Inability to hold integer data types

explanation: Arrays have a static capacity; resizing requires creating a new memory block and copying elements, costing O(N) time.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Consider an array int A[5][10][20] in C. How many total integer elements are allocated?
explanation: Total elements = 5 * 10 * 20 = 1000 integers.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In a sparse matrix with 1000 rows, 1000 columns, and only 500 non-zero entries, the 3-tuple array requires how many rows?
explanation: The 3-tuple requires 500 rows for the non-zero elements plus 1 header row storing (1000, 1000, 500), totaling 501 rows.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: What is the worst-case space complexity of recursive algorithms that recurse to depth N without extra dynamic allocations?
explanation: Each recursive call pushes an activation record onto the system call stack, consuming O(N) call stack space.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: If an algorithm requires O(1) auxiliary space, it is known as:
explanation: An in-place algorithm transforms input using no more than a constant O(1) amount of extra storage space.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: In C, the expression *(A + i) is mathematically equivalent to:
explanation: In C, array subscript notation A[i] is defined precisely as syntactic sugar for *(A + i).

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: When two matrices of sizes M x K and K x N are multiplied using standard nested loops, the time complexity is:
explanation: Standard matrix multiplication uses three nested loops running M, N, and K times, yielding O(M * K * N) operations.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which asymptotic notation is used when an algorithm's running time is strictly less than a bound (non-tight upper bound)?
explanation: Little-oh (o) defines a non-tight upper bound, meaning f(N) becomes insignificant compared to g(N) as N approaches infinity.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: Which data organization allows direct random access to any element using an offset calculation?
explanation: Arrays store items contiguously, enabling O(1) direct memory access using base + index * size.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: A band matrix with bandwidth k has non-zero elements located:

options.text: Only along the border rows and columns
Within a diagonal band of width k centered around the main diagonal

explanation: A band matrix has all non-zero entries confined within diagonal bands around the main diagonal.

unit_title: Introduction to Data Structures, Complexity & Arrays
prompt: The worst-case time complexity of finding the maximum element in an unsorted array of size N is:
explanation: In an unsorted array, every single element must be checked at least once, requiring N-1 comparisons, which is O(N).

prompt: What is the mandatory prerequisite before executing a Binary Search on an array?

options.text: The array must contain only positive integers
The array elements must be sorted in order
The array must be implemented as a linked list
The array size must be an exact power of 2

explanation: Binary search relies on divide-and-conquer and requires elements to be sorted in ascending or descending order.

prompt: What is the worst-case number of comparisons in Binary Search for an array of size N?
explanation: Binary search cuts the remaining search space in half at each step, taking at most floor(log2 N) + 1 comparisons.

prompt: In Linear Search, what is the average number of comparisons required to search for an item present in an array of size N?
explanation: Assuming uniform probability of element position, the average comparisons are (1 + 2 + ... + N) / N = (N + 1) / 2.

prompt: If an element is present at the first index of an array, what is the best-case time complexity of Linear Search?
explanation: When the target item is at index 0, linear search completes on the first comparison in O(1) time.

prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of Binary Search?
explanation: Even in the worst case (element absent or at the last comparison), binary search runs in O(log N) time.

prompt: Which searching algorithm is suitable for searching an item in an unsorted linked list?
explanation: Linked lists do not permit O(1) random middle access, so binary search cannot be applied efficiently; linear search must be used.

prompt: What is Hashing?

options.text: A sorting technique based on binary trees
A technique that maps keys to indices in a hash table using a mathematical function
A compression algorithm for text files
A method to balance AVL trees

explanation: Hashing transforms search keys into table array slots via a hash function, aiming for O(1) average lookup time.

prompt: What is a Hash Collision?

options.text: When two identical keys are inserted into different tables
When a hash function maps two distinct keys to the same table index
When the hash table runs out of memory

explanation: A collision occurs when h(k1) == h(k2) for two different keys k1 != k2.

prompt: In the division hash function h(k) = k mod m, what is the recommended choice for table size m?

options.text: A prime number not close to a power of 2

explanation: Selecting a prime number m minimizes common factors with keys, distributing hash values more uniformly.

prompt: Which hash function squares the key and extracts a specified number of middle digits?
explanation: The mid-square method squares the key (k^2) and takes the middle digits as the hash address.

prompt: In the folding method of hashing, how is the hash address generated?

options.text: The key is divided into parts, which are then combined (added) together
The key is multiplied by a floating-point constant
The key is repeatedly shifted left
The square root of the key is computed

explanation: Folding partitions the key into parts equal in size to the address length and adds them up to obtain the hash address.

prompt: Which collision resolution technique stores all colliding keys in an external linked list at each table index?
explanation: Separate chaining maintains a linked list of records that hash to the same bucket index.

prompt: What is Open Addressing in hashing?

options.text: All elements are stored directly inside the hash table array without linked lists
Hash keys are visible to external users
The hash function is public domain

explanation: In open addressing (closed hashing), all elements occupy slots within the table array itself.

prompt: In Linear Probing, if a collision occurs at index h, which slot is inspected next?
explanation: Linear probing scans sequentially: slot (h + i) mod m for probe sequence i = 0, 1, 2, ...

prompt: What major phenomenon degrades the performance of Linear Probing as table load factor increases?
explanation: Primary clustering occurs when long continuous runs of occupied slots build up, drastically increasing average probe lengths.

prompt: In Quadratic Probing, the probe sequence for collision resolution is defined by:
explanation: Quadratic probing uses a quadratic polynomial in i (typically i^2) to space out probes and prevent primary clustering.

prompt: Which open addressing method uses a second independent hash function to compute probe intervals?
explanation: Double hashing uses interval = h2(k), probing slots at (h1(k) + i * h2(k)) mod m.

prompt: What is the Load Factor (α) of a hash table with N stored keys and M total buckets?
explanation: Load factor α = N / M measures table fullness and dictates when resizing/rehashing is needed.

prompt: What is the ideal average-case search time complexity in a well-designed hash table?
explanation: With a uniform hash function and low load factor, search and insertion take O(1) expected time.

prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in a hash table using separate chaining when all N keys collide?
explanation: If all keys hash to the same bucket, the linked list degenerates into an O(N) linear search.

prompt: How does Insertion Sort build the sorted array?

options.text: By repeatedly finding the minimum element and placing it at the start
By repeatedly taking the next element and inserting it into its correct position in the already sorted sub-array
By dividing the array into halves and merging
By swapping adjacent elements that are out of order

explanation: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts the current element into its proper position among sorted items.

prompt: What is the best-case time complexity of Insertion Sort when the input array is already sorted?
explanation: When the array is already sorted, each element requires only 1 comparison and 0 shifts, taking O(N) time.

prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of Insertion Sort (e.g., when array is reverse sorted)?
explanation: For reverse-sorted arrays, the k-th element requires k comparisons and shifts, totaling N*(N-1)/2 = O(N^2) operations.

prompt: Which sorting algorithm performs the minimum number of memory swaps (at most N - 1 swaps)?
explanation: Selection sort makes at most 1 swap per pass (N - 1 swaps in total), making it ideal when write operations are expensive.

prompt: What is the time complexity of Selection Sort in the best, average, and worst cases?

options.text: O(N log N) in all cases
O(N) best case, O(N^2) worst case

explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion regardless of array order, making N*(N-1)/2 comparisons in every case: O(N^2).

prompt: Which algorithmic paradigm does Merge Sort utilize?
explanation: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the sorted halves.

prompt: What is the time complexity of Merge Sort in the worst case?
explanation: Merge sort always divides input evenly into 2 halves and takes O(N) to merge, running in O(N log N) in all cases.

prompt: What is the auxiliary space complexity of standard Merge Sort on an array of size N?
explanation: Standard merge sort requires a temporary auxiliary array of size N to merge elements.

prompt: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be 'Stable'?

options.text: It uses constant extra memory O(1)
It preserves the relative order of records with equal keys
It has O(N log N) worst-case time

explanation: Stability ensures duplicate key elements retain their original relative positions after sorting.

prompt: Which of the following sorting algorithms is inherently stable?
explanation: Standard merge sort preserves relative order during the merge step (using <= comparison), making it stable.

prompt: Trace Insertion Sort: What is the array state after inserting 2 into sorted sub-array [3, 7, 9]?
explanation: Elements 9, 7, and 3 shift right by one slot, and 2 is placed at index 0.

prompt: After the first pass of Selection Sort (ascending order) on [29, 10, 14, 37, 13], what is the array state?
explanation: The minimum element 10 is found and swapped with the first element 29.

prompt: What is the recurrence relation for Merge Sort?
explanation: Merge sort divides into 2 subproblems of size N/2 and performs an O(N) linear merge: T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N).

prompt: How many passes are required in Selection Sort to sort an array of N elements?
explanation: After placing the first N - 1 elements into their correct positions, the last element is automatically in place.

prompt: Which searching technique is the most efficient when elements are uniformly distributed in a sorted array?
explanation: Interpolation search estimates target position based on key value, achieving O(log log N) average time for uniformly distributed data.

prompt: What is Secondary Clustering in open addressing hashing?

options.text: Clustering that occurs when keys hash to different initial positions but follow the same probe sequence
Clustering of duplicate records in separate chaining
Clustering caused by poor hardware RAM

explanation: Secondary clustering happens in quadratic probing because all keys hashing to the same initial slot follow the exact same probe sequence.

prompt: What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to merge two sorted arrays of sizes M and N?
explanation: At each comparison, one element is output. The last remaining element does not need comparison, giving at most M + N - 1 comparisons.

prompt: Under what scenario is Insertion Sort preferred over Merge Sort?

options.text: When the array has billions of random elements
When the array is very small or nearly already sorted
When minimizing memory is not important
When worst-case guarantee of O(N log N) is strictly required

explanation: For small arrays (N < 20) or nearly sorted data, insertion sort has low overhead and runs in O(N) time with O(1) space.

prompt: Rehashing in a hash table involves:

options.text: Encrypting all stored keys with a secret cipher
Allocating a larger table (often double size) and re-inserting all keys using a new hash function
Converting the hash table into a binary search tree

explanation: When load factor exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.75), rehashing creates a bigger table and re-maps all existing entries.

prompt: Which sorting algorithm is typically used for external sorting when data exceeds available RAM?
explanation: External merge sort chunks data into memory-sized runs, sorts them, and merges them sequentially from disk.

prompt: Given hash table size 7 and hash function h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10, 17, 24 all hash to index:
explanation: 10 mod 7 = 3, 17 mod 7 = 3, and 24 mod 7 = 3. All three collide at slot 3.

prompt: Using Linear Probing on a table of size 7 with h(k) = k mod 7, where is key 24 placed after inserting 10 and 17?
explanation: 10 goes to slot 3. 17 collides at 3, probes (3+1) mod 7 = slot 4. 24 collides at 3 and 4, probes (3+2) mod 7 = slot 5.

prompt: What is the time complexity of searching an element in a sorted array of size 1,000,000 using Binary Search?
explanation: log2(1,000,000) is approximately 19.93, so at most 20 comparisons are needed.

prompt: Which hash collision resolution method is least affected by high load factors (load factor > 1)?
explanation: Separate chaining dynamically extends linked lists outside the table array, so it functions even when N > M.

prompt: If an algorithm compares every adjacent pair and swaps them if out of order, it is:
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.

prompt: How many comparisons does Selection Sort make on an array of 5 elements?
explanation: Comparisons = N*(N-1)/2 = 5*4/2 = 10 comparisons.

prompt: What is the lower bound of comparison-based sorting algorithms in the worst case?
explanation: Decision tree analysis proves that any comparison-based sort must make at least Ω(N log N) comparisons in the worst case.

prompt: A hash function that distributes keys evenly and independently across all slots satisfies:
explanation: The simple uniform hashing assumption states that any given key is equally likely to hash into any of the m slots.

prompt: When is a hash table search guaranteed to be O(1) in the worst case?

options.text: When linear probing is used with load factor 0.9
When using Perfect Hashing (with static key sets)
When table size is a power of 2

explanation: Perfect hashing designs a two-level hash table tailored for a known static key set, providing O(1) worst-case lookup.

prompt: Which property of Merge Sort makes it the preferred sorting algorithm for linked lists?

options.text: It requires zero extra memory when implemented on linked lists (O(1) auxiliary space)
It executes in O(N) time for linked lists

explanation: Merging linked lists involves only pointer manipulation without allocating new array blocks, making Merge Sort O(1) extra space for linked lists.

prompt: What operational principle governs a Stack data structure?
explanation: A Stack follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) discipline, where the most recently inserted element is removed first.

prompt: Which pointer variable tracks the top element in an array-based stack implementation?
explanation: The 'top' pointer holds the array index of the most recently inserted element in a stack.

prompt: In a stack of capacity MAX, what condition indicates a Stack Overflow during a push operation?
explanation: For a 0-indexed array of size MAX, when top == MAX - 1, the stack is completely full and cannot accept new items.

prompt: What condition signals a Stack Underflow during a pop operation in an empty stack?
explanation: When the stack contains no elements, top is initialized to -1. Attempting to pop causes stack underflow.

prompt: What does the Peek() or Top() stack operation do?

options.text: Inserts an element into the stack
Removes the top element and decreases top pointer
Returns the value of the top element without removing it
Clears all elements in the stack

explanation: Peek returns the top element's value while keeping the stack state and top index unchanged.

prompt: Which computer architecture component utilizes the stack mechanism extensively?

options.text: Function call / Activation record call stack

explanation: Program execution uses the runtime call stack to store return addresses, local variables, and parameters during function invocations.

prompt: What is the time complexity of Push and Pop operations in a standard stack?
explanation: Pushing and popping require only incrementing/decrementing the top pointer and one array assignment, taking O(1) time.

prompt: Which notation places the operator before its operands (e.g., + A B)?
explanation: In Prefix notation (invented by Jan Lukasiewicz), the operator precedes its operands: + A B.

prompt: Which notation places the operator after its operands (e.g., A B +)?
explanation: Postfix notation (Reverse Polish Notation) places the operator directly after its operands: A B +.

prompt: Why are Postfix and Prefix expressions advantageous for compiler evaluation?

options.text: They eliminate the need for parentheses and operator precedence rules
They take half the memory of infix expressions

explanation: Postfix and prefix expressions are unambiguous without parentheses, allowing straightforward single-pass evaluation via a stack.

prompt: What is the postfix form of the infix expression: (A + B) * C?
explanation: Due to parentheses, (A + B) becomes AB+. Then multiplying by C yields AB+ C *.

prompt: Convert the infix expression: A + B * C to postfix notation:
explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: B * C becomes BC*. Then A + BC* yields A BC* +.

prompt: What is the postfix evaluation algorithm's response when an operand (number) is encountered in the expression?

options.text: Push the operand onto the operand stack
Multiply it by the top value

explanation: When scanning a postfix expression, every encountered operand is immediately pushed onto the stack.

prompt: When an operator is encountered during postfix evaluation, what action is taken?

options.text: Push the operator onto the stack
Pop the top two operands, apply the operator, and push the result back

explanation: The operator pops operand 2 (top) and operand 1 (second from top), calculates (op1 <operator> op2), and pushes the result.

prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression: 6 3 2 + * 5 -
What is the prefix form of the infix expression: (A + B) / (C - D)?
explanation: (A + B) -> +AB; (C - D) -> -CD. Applying division: / (+AB) (-CD) = / + A B - C D.

prompt: Which operator has the highest precedence in standard arithmetic expression evaluation?
explanation: Exponentiation (^) has the highest precedence among basic arithmetic operators and associates from right to left.

prompt: What is the associativity of the exponentiation (^) operator in C / mathematical conventions?
explanation: Exponentiation evaluates right-to-left: 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 evaluates as 2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 2 ^ 9 = 512.

prompt: In infix to postfix conversion, what happens when a left parenthesis '(' is encountered?

options.text: It is immediately output to the postfix string
It is pushed onto the operator stack
It pops all operators from the stack

explanation: A left parenthesis '(' acts as an operator with high incoming priority and is pushed onto the stack.

prompt: In infix to postfix conversion, what happens when a right parenthesis ')' is encountered?

options.text: It is pushed onto the stack
Operators are popped from the stack and output until a '(' is popped and discarded
It is printed directly to the output

explanation: Encountering ')' triggers popping all operators within that parenthesized block until the matching '(' is removed.

prompt: What discipline governs a standard Queue data structure?
explanation: A Queue follows First In, First Out (FIFO): the first item inserted at the rear is the first item removed from the front.

prompt: In a linear queue, insertions take place at the _____ and deletions take place at the _____.
explanation: Insertions (enqueue) occur at the REAR end, while deletions (dequeue) occur at the FRONT end.

prompt: In a standard 0-indexed linear queue of size MAX, what condition indicates that the queue is empty?
explanation: Initially, an empty queue is represented by front = -1 and rear = -1.

prompt: What is the primary limitation of a standard Linear Queue implemented with a fixed array?

options.text: False Overflow: elements cannot be inserted even when free space exists at the front after deletions
Deletion requires shifting all elements every time

explanation: As rear reaches MAX-1, no new item can be enqueued even if previous slots were freed by dequeue operations.

prompt: How does a Circular Queue resolve the false overflow issue of linear queues?

options.text: By doubling the array size dynamically
By wrapping rear and front pointers back to index 0 using modulo arithmetic
By shifting all elements forward on every deletion

explanation: In a circular queue, rear = (rear + 1) % MAX wraps around to index 0 when reaching the end, reusing freed front slots.

prompt: In a circular queue of capacity MAX, what condition indicates that the queue is completely FULL?
explanation: A circular queue is full when advancing rear by one modulo MAX lands exactly on the front pointer.

prompt: What does Deque stand for?
explanation: A Deque (Double-Ended Queue) allows insertions and deletions at both the front and rear ends.

prompt: An Input-Restricted Deque is one where:

options.text: Insertion is allowed at only one end, while deletion is allowed at both ends
Deletion is allowed at only one end, while insertion is allowed at both ends

explanation: Input-restricted deques restrict insertion to a single end (e.g. rear) while permitting deletion from both front and rear.

prompt: An Output-Restricted Deque is one where:

options.text: Insertion is allowed at only one end
Deletion is allowed at only one end, while insertion is allowed at both ends

explanation: Output-restricted deques restrict deletions to one end while allowing insertions at both ends.

prompt: What is a Priority Queue?

options.text: A queue where elements are arranged in strictly FIFO order
A queue where each element has an assigned priority and higher priority items are served before lower priority ones
A queue stored on top of a stack
A queue with unlimited memory capacity

explanation: In a priority queue, elements are processed based on priority values rather than strictly their arrival order.

prompt: Which underlying data structure provides the most efficient implementation of a Priority Queue?
explanation: A Binary Heap (Min-Heap or Max-Heap) implements priority queue insertion and deletion in O(log N) time.

prompt: Which application relies primarily on a Queue data structure?

options.text: Undo operation in a text editor
Printer spooling and CPU job scheduling

explanation: Printer spooling and round-robin CPU scheduling process requests in first-come, first-served (FIFO) order via queues.

prompt: How many standard single-ended queues are required to implement a Stack?
explanation: A stack can be simulated using two queues by making either the push operation costly (O(N)) or the pop operation costly (O(N)).

prompt: How many standard stacks are required to implement a FIFO Queue?
explanation: A FIFO queue can be implemented using two stacks (one for enqueue and one for dequeue), giving amortized O(1) operations.

prompt: Which data structure is used to check for balanced parentheses in an expression like '{[()]} '?
explanation: A stack pushes opening brackets and pops them upon encountering closing brackets, checking for matching pairs.

prompt: In Tower of Hanoi puzzle with N disks, the minimum number of moves required is:
explanation: The recurrence relation M(N) = 2*M(N-1) + 1 yields 2^N - 1 total moves, solved using the system call stack.

prompt: What is the result of converting the infix expression 'A + B * (C - D)' to prefix?
explanation: (C - D) -> -CD; then B * -CD -> *B-CD; then A + (*B-CD) -> + A * B - C D.

prompt: When front == rear in a circular queue containing elements, what does it mean?

options.text: The queue contains exactly one element

explanation: In a 1-indexed or initialized circular queue, front == rear indicates that exactly one element remains.

prompt: What happens if you dequeue from an empty queue?

options.text: The front pointer is reset to 0

explanation: Attempting to remove an item from an empty queue triggers Queue Underflow.

prompt: Which traversal technique on a graph uses a Queue?
explanation: BFS explores vertices level by level using a FIFO queue, while DFS uses a LIFO stack.

prompt: Which traversal technique on a graph uses a Stack?
explanation: DFS explores branches as deeply as possible before backtracking, relying on a stack (or recursive call stack).

prompt: What is the value of the prefix expression '+ * 2 3 4'?
explanation: Evaluating prefix from right to left: * 2 3 = 6. Then + 6 4 = 10.

prompt: In C, which header file provides dynamic memory allocation functions (malloc/free) used to implement linked stacks?
explanation: <stdlib.h> declares malloc(), calloc(), realloc(), and free() needed for dynamic linked data structures.

prompt: What is the space complexity of converting an infix string of length N to postfix using a stack?
explanation: In the worst case (e.g. deeply nested parentheses), the operator stack stores up to O(N) operators.

prompt: A circular queue of capacity 6 currently has front = 4 and rear = 2. How many elements are in the queue?
explanation: Elements are stored at indices 4, 5, 0, 1, 2. Count = (rear - front + MAX) % MAX + 1 = (2 - 4 + 6) % 6 + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 elements.

prompt: Which data structure is ideal for implementing an 'Undo' and 'Redo' mechanism in software?

options.text: Two Stacks (Undo stack and Redo stack)

explanation: Actions are pushed onto an Undo stack; undoing pops the action and pushes it onto a Redo stack.

prompt: Can an array-based stack grow indefinitely without reallocation?

options.text: Yes, arrays in C are unbounded
No, fixed-size arrays have a static upper bound defined at creation

explanation: Static arrays have a fixed size; once top reaches MAX - 1, no further items can be stored without manual resizing.

prompt: In a min-priority queue, which element is removed first?

options.text: The element with the largest numerical key
The element with the smallest numerical key

explanation: In a min-priority queue, the item with the minimum key (highest logical priority) is dequeued first.

prompt: What is the time complexity of finding the maximum element in a standard LIFO stack of N elements?
explanation: A standard stack only exposes its top element; inspecting all elements requires popping all N items in O(N) time.

prompt: Which stack application evaluates recursive functions non-recursively?

options.text: Recursion elimination via an explicit user stack

explanation: Any recursive function can be transformed into an iterative algorithm by explicitly managing state on a user-defined stack.

prompt: What are the two essential fields of a node in a Singly Linked List?
explanation: Each node in a singly linked list contains a data element and a pointer ('next') referencing the subsequent node.

prompt: What value does the 'next' pointer of the last node in a linear singly linked list hold?
explanation: The last node's next pointer points to NULL, marking the termination of the linked list.

prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the beginning (head) of a singly linked list?
explanation: Inserting at head requires updating the new node's next pointer and reassigning head, taking O(1) constant time.

prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the end of a singly linked list with only a head pointer?
explanation: Without a tail pointer, the entire list must be traversed from head to the last node in O(N) time.

prompt: In a Doubly Linked List (Two-Way List), each node contains:

options.text: Data, Next pointer, and Random pointer
Data, Previous pointer, and Next pointer
Two data fields and one pointer

explanation: A doubly linked list node holds data, a pointer to the previous node ('prev'), and a pointer to the next node ('next').

prompt: What is the primary advantage of a Doubly Linked List over a Singly Linked List?

options.text: It uses less memory per node
It allows bidirectional traversal (both forward and backward)
It stores elements in contiguous memory

explanation: The 'prev' pointer permits backward navigation and O(1) node deletion when a direct node pointer is provided.

prompt: In a Circular Singly Linked List, where does the last node point to?
explanation: In a circular singly linked list, the final node's next pointer points back to the first node instead of NULL.

prompt: What is a Header Linked List?

options.text: A list stored in the program header
A linked list that contains a special header node at the beginning that stores metadata
A list containing only header files
A doubly linked list without data

explanation: A header linked list begins with a header node storing global list properties (e.g., node count, max/min values).

prompt: In a Grounded Header List, the last node points to:
explanation: In a grounded header list, the header node begins the list and the last node's link is set to NULL.

prompt: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in a singly linked list of N nodes?
explanation: Because nodes are linked sequentially without indexed addressing, search requires O(N) linear traversal.

prompt: In tree data structures, what is a Leaf Node (Terminal Node)?

options.text: The topmost node in the hierarchy
A node with exactly two children

explanation: A leaf node is a node with zero child nodes (out-degree 0).

prompt: What is the Degree of a tree node?

options.text: The distance from the root to the node
The number of subtrees (children) attached to the node
The total number of nodes in the tree

explanation: The degree of a node is the total number of its direct children.

prompt: In a Binary Tree, what is the maximum degree of any node?
explanation: By definition, every node in a binary tree has at most two children, typically termed left child and right child.

prompt: What is the maximum number of nodes at level L of a binary tree (assuming the root is at level 0)?
explanation: Level 0 has 2^0 = 1 node; level 1 has 2^1 = 2; level 2 has 2^2 = 4; level L has 2^L nodes.

prompt: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height H (where height of single node tree is 0)?
explanation: A full binary tree of height H has sum(2^0 + 2^1 + ... + 2^H) = 2^(H + 1) - 1 total nodes.

prompt: What is a Full (Strict / Proper) Binary Tree?

options.text: A tree where all leaves are at the exact same depth
A binary tree where every node has either 0 or 2 children
A tree where all nodes have 1 child

explanation: In a strict (full) binary tree, no node has exactly 1 child; every node has either 0 or 2 children.

prompt: What is a Complete Binary Tree?

options.text: A binary tree where every level except possibly the last is completely full, and all nodes in the last level are as far left as possible
A tree where all nodes have 2 children
A tree that has no leaves

explanation: A complete binary tree fills all levels completely except possibly the last, where leaves fill from left to right.

prompt: What is the relationship between the number of leaf nodes (L) and nodes with two children (N2) in any binary tree?
explanation: In any non-empty binary tree, the number of leaf nodes L is always exactly one greater than the number of internal nodes with degree two: L = N2 + 1.

prompt: What is the minimum height of a binary tree containing N nodes?
explanation: The minimum height occurs when the tree is completely balanced, yielding height = floor(log2 N).

prompt: What is the maximum height of a degenerate (skewed) binary tree containing N nodes?
explanation: In a skewed binary tree where every node has only 1 child, the tree degenerates into a linked list of height N - 1.

prompt: In which traversal order is a binary tree visited as: Left Subtree -> Root -> Right Subtree?
explanation: Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, processes the root node, and then visits the right subtree (LNR).

prompt: In which traversal order is a binary tree visited as: Root -> Left Subtree -> Right Subtree?
explanation: Preorder traversal visits the root node first, followed by the left and right subtrees (NLR).

prompt: In which traversal order is a binary tree visited as: Left Subtree -> Right Subtree -> Root?
explanation: Postorder traversal visits both child subtrees before processing the root node (LRN).

prompt: Which traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST) produces elements in strictly ascending sorted order?
explanation: Since BST enforces Left < Root < Right, inorder traversal (LNR) naturally yields elements in non-decreasing sorted order.

prompt: Given a binary tree with root A, left child B, and right child C, what is the Preorder traversal?
explanation: Preorder = Root, Left, Right = A, B, C.

prompt: Given a binary tree with root A, left child B, and right child C, what is the Postorder traversal?
explanation: Postorder = Left, Right, Root = B, C, A.

prompt: Can a binary tree be uniquely reconstructed given its Inorder and Preorder traversals?

options.text: Only if it is a complete binary tree
Only if all keys are negative

explanation: Preorder identifies root nodes, while Inorder splits elements into left and right subtrees, allowing unique reconstruction.

prompt: Can a binary tree be uniquely reconstructed using only Preorder and Postorder traversals?

options.text: No, not in general (unless the tree is strictly full)
Only if the tree is skewed

explanation: Without Inorder traversal, Preorder + Postorder cannot uniquely distinguish between a left-child-only node and a right-child-only node.

prompt: What is the time complexity of traversing a binary tree with N nodes using recursive inorder traversal?
explanation: Every node is visited exactly once, requiring O(N) time.

prompt: What is the auxiliary space complexity of recursive binary tree traversal on a balanced tree?
explanation: The recursion stack depth is equal to tree height; for a balanced tree, height is O(log N).

prompt: To delete the first node of a non-empty singly linked list, which pointer assignment is executed?
explanation: Save head in temp, advance head = head->next, and release memory with free(temp).

prompt: How can a cycle (loop) in a singly linked list be detected in O(N) time and O(1) space?

options.text: Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare with two pointers)

explanation: Floyd's algorithm uses a slow pointer (1 step) and fast pointer (2 steps); if they meet, a cycle exists.

prompt: What is the time complexity of reversing a singly linked list in-place?
explanation: Reversing pointers using three tracking pointers (prev, curr, next) visits each node once in O(N) time and O(1) space.

prompt: In a circular doubly linked list with head pointer, what does head->prev point to?

options.text: The last node in the list
The second node in the list

explanation: In a circular doubly linked list, head->prev points directly to the tail node, and tail->next points to head.

prompt: What is an Extended Binary Tree (2-Tree)?

options.text: A binary tree with 4 children per node
A binary tree where every null subtree is replaced by an external special node

explanation: An extended binary tree replaces all empty subtrees with special square external nodes, transforming it into a strict binary tree.

prompt: In an extended binary tree with E external nodes and I internal nodes, what is the relation?
explanation: Since external nodes are leaf nodes and all internal nodes have degree 2: E = I + 1.

prompt: Which traversal visits binary tree nodes level by level from top to bottom and left to right?
explanation: Level-order traversal uses a FIFO queue to visit nodes horizontally across each depth level.

prompt: How many null pointers exist in a binary tree with N nodes implemented with left and right child pointers?
explanation: Total pointers = 2N. Each node except root has 1 incoming edge (N - 1 edges). Null pointers = 2N - (N - 1) = N + 1.

prompt: What is a Threaded Binary Tree?

options.text: A tree executing on multi-core CPU threads
A binary tree that utilizes null pointers to store in-order predecessor or successor references
A tree with string data types
A binary tree without a root node

explanation: Threaded binary trees replace NULL pointers with direct threads to inorder predecessors/successors, enabling stackless traversal.

prompt: What is the time complexity of finding the middle element of a singly linked list in a single pass?
explanation: Using two pointers where fast advances 2 nodes and slow advances 1 node reaches the middle in N/2 iterations = O(N).

prompt: What is the base case in a recursive algorithm to compute the height of a binary tree?

options.text: if (root == NULL) return -1; (or 0 depending on convention)

explanation: When root is NULL, recursion terminates and returns -1 (for height in edges) or 0 (for height in nodes).

prompt: The recursive function: int count(Node* root) { if(!root) return 0; return 1 + count(root->left) + count(root->right); } computes:

options.text: The total number of nodes in the binary tree
The number of leaf nodes only
The sum of all key values

explanation: This recursive algorithm counts the current node (1) plus all nodes in left and right subtrees.

prompt: In a complete binary tree stored as an array with 1-based indexing, the left child of node at index i is at:
explanation: In 1-based array representation: Left_Child(i) = 2*i, Right_Child(i) = 2*i + 1, Parent(i) = floor(i / 2).

prompt: In a complete binary tree stored as an array with 1-based indexing, the parent of node at index i is at:
explanation: For any node at index i > 1, its parent resides at index floor(i / 2).

prompt: What is an Inorder Predecessor in a binary tree?

options.text: The node that precedes the current node in an inorder traversal sequence

explanation: The inorder predecessor is the node visited immediately before the given node in inorder (LNR) order.

prompt: In a Binary Search Tree, where is the Inorder Predecessor of a node with a left child located?

options.text: The leftmost node in the right subtree
The rightmost node in the left subtree

explanation: In a BST, the largest value smaller than the node resides at the rightmost position of its left subtree.

prompt: What is the expression tree representation of '(A + B) * C'?

options.text: A binary tree with root '*', left child as a subtree with root '+' and leaves A, B, and right child C
A single linked list with 5 nodes

explanation: An expression tree places operators at internal nodes and operands at leaf nodes; '*' is the top operator.

prompt: In a doubly linked list, what is required to delete node 'curr' given its direct pointer?
explanation: Updating surrounding pointers bypasses 'curr' in O(1) time without traversing the list from head.

prompt: What is the maximum number of leaves in a binary tree of height H?
explanation: At maximum depth H, the tree can have at most 2^H leaves.

prompt: Which traversal is suitable for deleting/freeing all nodes of a binary tree in C without dangling pointers?
explanation: Postorder deletes both children subtrees first before freeing the root node, preventing memory access errors.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What property characterizes a Binary Search Tree (BST)?

options.text: Left subtree keys <= Root key <= Right subtree keys
All keys must be prime numbers
A node can have three children

explanation: In a BST, every key in the left subtree is strictly less than the root, and every key in the right subtree is strictly greater.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the worst-case search time complexity in a skewed Binary Search Tree of N nodes?
explanation: When keys are inserted in sorted order, the BST degenerates into a linear chain of height N, taking O(N) search time.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Who invented the AVL Tree in 1962?
explanation: Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis published the first self-balancing binary search tree in 1962.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the definition of the Balance Factor of a node in an AVL Tree?

options.text: Number of left nodes + Number of right nodes
Depth of the node / Total nodes

explanation: Balance Factor (BF) = Height(Left_Subtree) - Height(Right_Subtree).

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What are the only permitted Balance Factor values for any node in an AVL tree?
explanation: To maintain height balance, every node in an AVL tree must strictly satisfy BF in {-1, 0, +1}.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching, insertion, and deletion in an AVL tree of N nodes?
explanation: Because AVL trees strictly maintain a height of O(log N), search, insert, and delete all run in guaranteed O(log N) worst-case time.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which rotation is performed when an insertion is made into the Left subtree of the Left child of node A (LL case)?
explanation: An LL imbalance is resolved with a single Right Rotation around the pivot node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which rotation is performed when an insertion is made into the Right subtree of the Right child of node A (RR case)?
explanation: An RR imbalance is resolved with a single Left Rotation around the pivot node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which combination of rotations resolves an LR imbalance in an AVL tree?

options.text: Left rotation on left child, then Right rotation on root node
Right rotation on right child, then Left rotation on root

explanation: An LR imbalance requires a double rotation: first Left-rotate the left child, then Right-rotate the critical node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which combination of rotations resolves an RL imbalance in an AVL tree?

options.text: Right rotation on right child, then Left rotation on root node
Left rotation on left child, then Right rotation on root

explanation: An RL imbalance requires a double rotation: first Right-rotate the right child, then Left-rotate the critical node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 0 (single node)?
explanation: Height 0 requires 1 node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the recurrence relation for the minimum number of nodes N(h) in an AVL tree of height h?
explanation: Minimum nodes N(h) = N(h - 1) + N(h - 2) + 1 (Fibonacci-like growth), ensuring height never exceeds 1.44 * log2 N.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 3?

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is an M-Way Search Tree?

options.text: A tree where each node can have at most M children and M - 1 keys
A binary tree with M roots

explanation: An M-way search tree of order M allows up to M children and M - 1 sorted keys per node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In an M-way search tree node containing k keys, how many subtrees can it point to?
explanation: k keys partition the key space into k + 1 distinct subtrees.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Why are multi-way trees (like B-Trees) preferred over binary search trees for disk-based storage?

options.text: Their high branching factor (fan-out) drastically reduces tree height, minimizing expensive disk I/O operations
They sort data in reverse order

explanation: Disk I/O is millions of times slower than RAM; a shallow multi-way tree minimizes block reads to 3 or 4 levels.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is a B-Tree of order M?

options.text: A self-balancing M-way search tree optimized for external storage systems
A binary tree with balance factor M
A tree where each node has exactly M keys
A tree that stores only booleans

explanation: Invented by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight, a B-tree is a balanced multi-way search tree with guaranteed balance properties.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order M, what is the maximum number of children any internal node can have?
explanation: By definition of order M, no node can have more than M children.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order M, what is the maximum number of keys an internal node can store?
explanation: A node with at most M children can store at most M - 1 keys.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order M, what is the minimum number of children for any internal node (other than root)?
explanation: All non-root internal nodes must be at least half full, possessing at least ceil(M / 2) children.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order M, what is the minimum number of keys in any non-root node?
explanation: Since an internal node has at least ceil(M / 2) children, it must contain at least ceil(M / 2) - 1 keys.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order 5, what is the maximum number of keys a node can hold before splitting?
explanation: Maximum keys = M - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4 keys.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B-Tree of order 5, what is the minimum number of keys for a non-root node?
explanation: ceil(5/2) = 3 children minimum, requiring at least 3 - 1 = 2 keys.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Where are all leaf nodes located in a B-Tree?

options.text: All leaves are strictly at the exact same depth/level
Leaves alternate between even and odd levels

explanation: A fundamental structural invariant of B-Trees is that all leaves are at the exact same bottom level.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: When inserting a key into a full B-Tree node, what operation occurs?

options.text: Node Splitting: the median key moves up to the parent, and remaining keys form two sibling nodes

explanation: Node overflow causes splitting: the median key promotes to the parent, dividing left and right halves into distinct nodes.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: How does a B-Tree grow in height?

options.text: Upward from the root when the root splits

explanation: Unlike binary trees which grow downward, a B-Tree grows upward when its root splits, creating a new root.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the key difference between a B-Tree and a B+ Tree?

options.text: B+ trees store all actual data records/pointers in leaf nodes, and leaf nodes are linked sequentially

explanation: In B+ trees, internal nodes store only index guide keys, all records reside in leaves, and leaves are linked for fast range queries.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Why are B+ Trees overwhelmingly preferred over B-Trees for relational database indexes (like MySQL InnoDB)?

options.text: Sequential range scans are O(K) fast by traversing the linked leaf list without tree traversals

explanation: Linked leaves allow range queries (e.g., WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30) to perform contiguous sequential reads.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is Multilevel Indexing?

options.text: Creating an index on an index to reduce searching within large index files

explanation: When an index file grows too large to fit in memory, a primary index is created over the secondary index file.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is a Dense Index?

options.text: An index entry appears for every search key value in the data file
An index stored on optical media
An index with duplicate keys omitted

explanation: In a dense index, an index record exists for every single search key value in the database file.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is a Sparse Index (in database indexing)?

options.text: An index with only zero keys
An index record appears for only some of the search keys (typically one per data block)

explanation: A sparse index creates one index entry per disk block, requiring less memory than a dense index.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the minimum number of keys a root node in a B-Tree can hold?
explanation: The root is exempt from the half-full rule and can contain as few as 1 key (and 2 children).

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: During deletion from a B-Tree, if a node falls below the minimum key count, what happens?

options.text: Borrowing a key from a sibling node (redistribution) or merging with a sibling

explanation: Underflow is resolved by borrowing a key from an immediate sibling or merging with a sibling through the parent.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In an AVL tree, after inserting keys 10, 20, 30 in order, what rotation is required?
explanation: Inserting 10, 20, 30 produces a right-skewed chain with BF(10) = -2 (RR case), resolved by a Left rotation on 10.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: After left-rotating 10 in the sequence 10, 20, 30, which node becomes the new root?
explanation: 20 becomes the root with 10 as its left child and 30 as its right child (both with BF = 0).

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In an AVL tree, after inserting keys 30, 10, 20 in order, which rotation is needed?
explanation: 10 is left child of 30, and 20 is right child of 10. This is an LR imbalance requiring an LR double rotation.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the height of an AVL tree with 7 nodes in the worst case?
explanation: Since N(3) = 7, 7 nodes can achieve a maximum height of 3.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the maximum number of keys in a B-Tree of order 4 and height 2 (root at height 0)?
explanation: Level 0: 3 keys. Level 1: 4*3=12 keys. Level 2: 16*3=48 keys. Total = 3 + 12 + 48 = 63 keys.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which self-balancing binary search tree uses color bits (Red and Black) instead of explicit balance factors?
explanation: Red-Black trees use a color bit per node to ensure no path is more than twice as long as any other path.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a 2-3 Tree (which is a B-Tree of order 3), every internal node contains:

options.text: Either 1 or 2 keys, and either 2 or 3 children

explanation: A 2-3 tree is a B-tree of order 3: a 2-node has 1 key & 2 children; a 3-node has 2 keys & 3 children.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is a 2-3-4 Tree?

options.text: A B-Tree of order 4 where nodes have 2, 3, or 4 children

explanation: A 2-3-4 tree is a B-tree of order 4, capable of holding up to 3 keys and 4 children per node.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the balance factor of a leaf node in an AVL tree?
explanation: A leaf node has left height 0 and right height 0 (or -1 and -1), so BF = 0 - 0 = 0.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the time complexity of a B-Tree search on disk if the tree has height h?
explanation: Disk accesses = O(h); within each node, binary search takes O(log M). Total time = O(h * log M).

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In an AVL tree, insertion requires at most how many rotations to restore balance?

options.text: At most 1 single or double rotation

explanation: Inserting into an AVL tree requires at most one single or double rotation to restore balance globally.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In an AVL tree, deletion may require at most how many rotations to restore balance?

options.text: O(log N) rotations (rebalancing may propagate up to the root)

explanation: Unlike insertion, an AVL deletion can reduce a subtree height, potentially triggering up to O(log N) rotations along the path to the root.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which index type is clustered in a database?

options.text: An index whose search key specifies the physical sequential order of records in the data file
A primary key index stored offsite

explanation: A clustered index physically orders table data pages on disk matching the index key sequence.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Can a table have multiple clustered indexes?

options.text: No, at most one clustered index per table because data rows can only be physically sorted one way
Only if columns are foreign keys

explanation: Because data records can only be stored in one physical sequence on disk, only one clustered index can exist per table.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: In a B+ tree, internal nodes act purely as:

options.text: A routing / index search guide to direct searches to the correct leaf node

explanation: Internal nodes in a B+ tree contain router keys that direct traversals to data blocks residing in leaves.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: What is the primary benefit of maintaining sequential leaf links in a B+ tree?

options.text: Enables fast sequential and range scanning without re-traversing the tree hierarchy
Reduces disk file size to zero

explanation: Leaves form a doubly or singly linked list, allowing fast O(K) sequential scanning once the start key is found.

unit_title: AVL Trees, M-way Search Trees & B-Trees
prompt: Which data structure is best suited for implementing a database indexing system where fast range queries are crucial?
explanation: B+ Trees provide both logarithmic point lookups and high-speed linear range scans, making them the industry standard for database indexing.
